interactions.title: The incomplete mural of the Sentient Ocean
lines: DM: ((Setup)) So you see, there's this, like, scholar merfolk woman and her 2 bound elementals you're trying to avoid, and they seem to be close, you know, roughly finishing up for the day and— and they— you know, there's the—the merfolk don’t have a written language. There's no—there's no paper anywhere. The ink doesn't really work underwater. What she seems to be sorting is a series of pictographs and mosaics. And so there's like a series of these piled up, piled all around the the room that she's working in that are like these depictions of whirlpools with like strange forms coming out of them. Different colored kind of glyphs that are not in a language, right? They're like symbols, right? They're like markers of some alien being or something like that. You, you, you—your Eyes of the Rune Keeper give you enough insight to, to realize that some of these are, are depicting names, strange names that you wouldn't know how to pronounce.

DM: And they seem to be names of— it's hard to know what of, actually— not people. Possibly names of places on wherever this sentient ocean life form came from. But it all seems very alien. And there's nothing written down. There's just these giant, like, very carefully pieced together, glued together, large, like, person-sized rock and coral, smooth walls that have these pictographs carved into them.
Delwath: Like a map? Or is it like a story?

DM: It's like a story. It's like, it's like— hi, it's like, sort of— it's not—it's not complete by any means. It seems—this seems to be like one quarter, one, or even less of the full thing, which must have been a giant, like, story sort of shown on a massive wall, or something like that.

DM: Strange, yeah, yeah. And it's hard to piece together what the story is, because it's not complete. But that's basically the—it's—it almost seems like it's—they're trying to reconstruct, like, a temple wall.
DM: Tells the story of how the sentient ocean got to Taelgar. Right. So with that we turn to Milo's story.

before: DM: You made your way into this strange prison complex by dispelling the bubble that was field around that, snuck through the darkness and made telepathic contact with Wellby’s halfling telepathy with Milo. I'm totally blanking on his name now: Milo Thistlefoot, who had been captured. You have been tracking him.

DM: And for kind of simplicity, and just to get things moving—and you had a short conversation with him. I'll use my intro to kind of tell his story, but it's close to the end of the shift, basically. And so he suggests to you that should you wish to, you know, free him and the other halflings, and and Tilly Brineheart, who's a spellcaster, the thing to do would be to swim up to the up to the, like, prison cells, once the—once the thing quiets in, like, half an hour, once it’s quieted down for the night, and there you would have a better chance to free them. So I think, unless anybody objects, we’d just assume you wait quietly for half an hour.
Delwath: The only thing I wanted to do is go read what's inside the hut.
after: DM: Underwater, transformed into a half-shark creature, forced to sort through debris, coral, and rock for fragments of ancient history. Milo thinks back and tells the tale to Wellby of how it all started.

DM: And it started with a journey, as it always does, a journey that had been quite a joy, actually. The Stormdancer had left Cedrano early in the spring, over a year ago now, heading south. In a month they were south of Illoria; in two, sailing through the strange waters of the Sea of Storms, dodging wind and rain, and passing arcane islands dotted with ancient ruins. Then months of sailing strange coastline, seeing the vast gleaming city of gold, islands of living bridges connected by great vines growing across channels, bustling markets full of the most tempting smells and strange fruits. And by the time they turned north the Stormdancer's hold was full of delicacies, and their hearts full of strange tales of the South.

DM: But of course no one would ever sail a straight journey back, and they'd already come to the canal by the time they reached the southern parts of Illoria again. Milo had heard tale of a fallen star in the mangrove swamps on the west coast of Apporia that lit up the lagoons at night, and so, of course, like any good sailor in his telling, they went that way: the long western route, instead of the short route to the canal.
DM: And it was that long journey that brought— sorry, hold on— that brought the Stormdancer to the silent sea, the dead calm of the city of Omi and everything that came next.

DM: And he was asleep, Milo says, when they hit the doldrums. Tilly was on watch, and we didn't really think anything of it at first. I mean, everybody encounters strange patches of the ocean here and again, don't they? But it was only when Tilly's magic could not seem to affect the water beneath them at all that Milo thought, hmm, there's something worth investigating here.
